(Context is photography; for RSVPs say only that state or territory laws may also apply.)

Australian Cyber Security Centre, cyber.gov.au, 'Learn about phishing scams' (no last-updated date shown, read 23 November 2026): 'Quishing is a type of phishing that uses QR codes instead of text-based links. QR codes are often trusted, but cybercriminals can use them to hide harmful links.'

cyber.gov.au (same page): 'Quishing is harder to detect than normal phishing because QR codes are images, not text. This means security tools may miss harmful links and you can’t check the link before scanning it.'

insider_details.detail: A reminder list holds guests' names, addresses and phone numbers, which OAIC gives as examples of personal information. Send each reminder to the one guest (or household) it is for rather than one group message that shows everyone's details, and keep the list somewhere you trust. General information as at November 2026, not legal advice.

OAIC says the Privacy Act doesn't cover individuals acting in a personal capacity, and that state or territory laws may apply in some situations. Phrase this as general information as at November 2026, not legal advice; do not state that any law does or does not apply to a couple's reminders.

If a printed reminder card or message carries a QR code to the RSVP page, print the RSVP web address beside it too. The Australian Cyber Security Centre notes scammers can use QR codes to hide harmful links and that you can't check a QR link before scanning it, so a typed address gives cautious guests another way in.

Timing advice (send a gentle reminder ahead of the couple's own reply date, then a personal follow-up to anyone still missing) is planning advice, not a sourced fact. Express it relative to the couple's reply date with no day counts or statistics, as 00-input.json directs.
